lawyer:
Syed Mahmood Hossain, Advocate — For the Petitioners. 
Khorshed Alam Khan, Advocate — For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Patit Paban Dey Mondal and others ------ Petitioners
Vs. 
Dulal Chandra Kundu Podder and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule by the pre-emptees-petitioners is directed against the judgment and order dated 12-3-1996 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Magura, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 38 of 1992 reversing those dated 24-10-92 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Salika within district Magura in Miscellaneous Case No. 50 of 1984. 

 2. The short facts of the case are that, the petitioner's father provash Chandra Kundu Podder and opposite party No. 2 are full brothers. Provash Chandra Kundu Podder died leaving petitioner No. 1 and Dulal Kundu Podder and opposite party Nos. 3-6 as heirs. Opposite party No. 2 sold the case land to opposite party No. 1 by a registered kabala dated 31-7-83 without giving notice to the petitioner and other co-sharers. Petitioner did not know of sale and after knowing the same he filed an application for pre-emption of the case land as co-sharer. Opposite party No. 1 contested the case by filing written statement stating that the petitioner knew's of the sale from the very beginning and petitioner No. 1 father requested the petitioner to purchase the case land but he refused. Petitioner No. 2 (pre-emptor No. 19) by filing separate written objection also supported above statement made in the written objection by opposite party No. 1. The learned Assistant Judge rejected the application and on appeal by the petitioner the learned Additional District Judge allowed the appeal and the pre-emption petition. Being dissatisfied with the order of the learned Additional District Judge the petitioner preferred this application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule. 

 3. Mr. Syed Mahmood Hossain, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the learned Additional District Judge framed no issue in respect of the limitation of the original petition and that the opposite party No. 2 is the benamder of his father who by filing a Title Suit No. 213 of 1985 got decree against the opposite party No. 1 and that the right, title of the suit land vest in opposite party No. 1. I have gone through the judgment of the courts below and found that there is no allegation about limitation of filing of petition made by the opposite party in their written statement and neither the trial Court nor the appellate Court in their judgment discussed the matter after framing an issue as the question of limitation was not raised at all. Further, the pre-emption case is filed in 1984 and the suit for declaration of benamder is filed in 1985 ie, long after he filed the pre-emption case. The opposite party did not file the judgment of the suit No. 213 of 1985 to satisfy the court as to that the opposite party No.1 was benamder is of the case land. Again, we find that before filing the suit for declaration the case land has already been transferred by the person against whom decree of benamder is alleged to have been obtained. Moreover, the courts below did not touch this point in their judgments. These two matters are questions of fact and this Court cannot raise this issue in its revisional jurisdiction. So, we find no substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner on these two points. Mr. Syed Mahmood Hossain further submits that the petitioner knew of sale of the case land and he was present at the time of registration of sale deed and did not purchase the case land on request of opposite party No. 2 and he waived his right of pre-emption by the aforesaid action. He again submits that the preemptor is the loco parentis with the pre-emptees and in such a case principle of estoppel is applicable. In support of his above submission he relied on a decision reported in 38 DLR 371 (Maulana Abdul Karim vs. Nur Jahan Begum & others) wherein His Lordship Mostafa Kamal J observed. 

 4. He also relied on a decision reported in 14 BLD (AD) 20 (Akhlasur Rahman and others vs. Safurullah and others) wherein their Lordships held: "That the pre-emptor took a leading part in bringing about the transaction; he assisted the sellers in selling the land, encouraged the buyers to purchase it and himself negotiated the price. In our opinio, this conduct of the pre-emptor was reasonably sufficient to give rise to waiver and acquiescence, and thus, estoppel will operate in any case. Because, the conduct of the Pre-emptor has induced the purchasers (appellants) to alter their position and the pre-emptor cannot now turn round and assert his right to undo a transaction which is very large with the result of his own creation." 

 5. This case is not identical to the present case. In this case the pre-emptor took part and assisted the seller in selling the land and encouraged the petitioner to purchase the same and negotiated fixing the price of land and that the same circumstance are not present in this instant case. In the case it is found that the DWs deposed that the petitioner was present at the time of purchase. There is no statement that the petitioner was requested to purchase the land by opposite party No. 2 and he refused to purchase the same or he was present at the time of execution and registration of the Kabala in question. In reply to the above submission Mr. Khorshed Alam Khan, the learned Advocate for the opposite party submitted that mere knowledge of purchase is not sufficient to waive the statutory right of the pre-emptor ie the present petitioner. In supporting the judgment of the appellate Court he also relied on a decision reported in 44 DLR (AD) 62 (Fazaruddin vs. Maijuddin and others). In the above case the learned Judges of the Appellate Division observed "as follows: 

 "It is true, the right of pre-emption accrues after transfer of the land, and statutory right of pre-emption cannot be taken away by mere verbal assurance of the persons having such right, unless other facts and circumstance clearly make out a case of acquiescence of waiver, Acquiescence arises when a person knowing that he is entitled to enforce some right neglects to do so for such a long time that the other person opposing such right may fairly infer that he has waived or abandoned it. It is failure to object to certain transaction or act. Waiver means simply abandonment of any claim or right." 

 6. The learned Assistant Judge rejected the petition on observing that the petitioner has not been corroborated as he did not give any other witnesses. But the Additional District Judge after discussing all the points and relying on a decision quoted above observed that the petitioner's right to pre-empt is not barred by acquiescence and waiver. Pre-emptor''s right is waived, if the pre-emptor took active part in selling the case land and became present when the purchaser took possession and did some things on a case land, but in the present case only fact before us is, that the petitioner is present at the time of purchase of the suit land. Mere presence or knowledge at the time of purchase cannot take away the statutory right of a pre-emptor to pre-empt the land by the principle of acquiescence and waiver. So, I find no substance in the submission made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner and also in this petition.
